turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Mr Naidoo, come through, sorry the clinic ran late. What brings you in today?

[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Ag it's fine, I had the newspaper. I'm here about this left hand, doctor, it's still not right after the stroke, three months now, and my wife said I mustn't skip the check even though she couldn't get off work.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Three months after a mild stroke. Tell me what the hand actually won't do.

[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): It's the left one, not dead, I can open and close it, but the grip is soft. Buttons take me ten minutes on the edge of the bed, and a full coffee cup tilts if I'm not watching it. It's been like that since I left the hospital, maybe a tiny bit better than month one, then it just plateaued.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): So it isn't marching on. I'm thinking residual weakness from that small stroke rather than a new event, but I won't commit till I've heard the rest. How is the walking?

[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Walking is fine, honestly, I don't drag the foot and I don't use a stick. Every morning I go to the robot on Milner Road and back, slow, but I'm 67 in July so some of that is just age. My wife watches from the stoep like I'm a toddler, shame.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): And speech? Any slurring, or words that won't come?

[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): No slurring. Speech is okay, my wife says I still talk too much, which, well, you can hear. Sometimes a name sits on the tip of my tongue, a neighbour or a tablet, and I wait a second and it comes, mostly when I'm tired. That's been there about two months, from a month after the stroke, not every day.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): That tip-of-the-tongue thing can linger. Any headaches with it?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No headaches. I don't get them, I never really have, even before all this.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. Any fevers these last weeks, even a low one?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No, no fever. I check with the grandkids' digital thermometer when I get bored and it sits around 36 point something. So definitely no.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Has your weight shifted at all?

[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm. I don't know. I haven't stood on a scale, and my brown trousers feel looser at the waist, or maybe I hung them wrong, and if I guessed I'd say a kilo, maybe two, but I couldn't tell you when that started.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll leave that a bit loose then. Any cough, or shortness of breath on that walk?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No cough. Breathing is fine, even up the little hill by the church, I don't get puffed.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me feel the grip while we talk. Squeeze. Hmm, left grip is a bit down on the right, nothing dramatic, and listening to you now there is no slurring.
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, soft but there. The index finger and the thumb are the lazy ones, the rest sort of follow.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): What tablets are you actually swallowing? The stroke ones and the pressure.

[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Three, I know them off by heart. Aspirin 75 milligrams, one in the morning by mouth, to keep the blood thin after the clot. The cholesterol one, I always say atorvastin, I mean atorvastatin, 40 milligrams at night, also by mouth. And amlodipine 5 milligrams in the morning for the blood pressure, with the aspirin, after porridge, and my wife packs the weekly box so I don't miss them.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Aspirin 75, atorvastatin 40 at night, amlodipine 5. That hangs together. Ever had a reaction to a medicine, a rash, swelling, anything?

[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, this part I'm not sure of, and I don't want to mislead you. Years back at Victoria Hospital, a chest infection, they gave me an antibiotic and also a painkiller for my back, and I came out in a red itchy rash on my chest and arms. Nobody told me which one did it, so maybe the antibiotic or the painkiller, I honestly don't know, and I've been nervous of both ever since.
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh, and penicillin I've had since, for a tooth, and that was fine, so maybe it wasn't penicillin. I still can't say which of those two it was.

[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ag, that's messy. We can't pin the rash on one drug and I'm not going to guess. I'll note a possible reaction to an antibiotic or a painkiller, unconfirmed, and I won't reach for either of those today.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sit quiet for me, I'm taking the pressure. Okay. 152 over 94. Pulse is 72, nice and regular.

[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): 152, hmm. At home on the Clicks machine I'm usually more like one thirty over 80, and I rushed in with a large coffee. The sister last time muttered about a white coat thing. There's a morning problem I should tell you, but carry on, doctor.

[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): 152 over 94 is higher than I want this far out from a stroke. I'm going to add a water tablet, hydrochlorothiazide 12.5 milligrams in the morning, on top of the amlodipine. That usually drops it a notch.

[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Before you write that, the morning thing, my wife said don't leave it out. When I stand up from the bed, maybe four mornings a week, the room goes swimmy, light-headed, a few seconds, and it clears if I hold the cupboard. No fall, so I didn't mention it, because it passes.

[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): And, doctor, I know I said no headaches, but that wasn't quite true. In the afternoons if I've overdone it, the left side of my head throbs, mild, and I just sit, I take nothing. I thought it didn't count. It's not a proper migraine like my sister gets.

[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ah. That changes the plan. If you're already light-headed on standing, a water tablet can drop you on the floor. Scratch the hydrochlorothiazide, I'm not starting it, and the amlodipine stays at 5 milligrams.

[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): So no new tablet. Is the swimmy feeling the stroke or the amlodipine? I've been on it since before the stroke, the GP in Plumstead started it when the pressure was found high, about six years now, and it's still ongoing.

[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): I can't split those cleanly today. Amlodipine can cause that postural drop, and so can standing up fast. This is not a new stroke on what you've told me. The hand fits a residual deficit from the mild stroke, and the afternoon head throb sounds more like fatigue, though I'm not calling that part certain.

[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): They said mild, a small clot on the right side of the brain, that's why the left hand, they explained it at Groote Schuur. I was in three days, no operation, they didn't cut anything. Speech was a bit thick the first day then it cleared, and walking was already okay by day two.

[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): No operation, that matches a straightforward clot. I was going to send you for an MRI because of the headaches you just owned up to. But they're mild, the weakness hasn't progressed, walking and speech are stable, so I'm changing my mind, no scan. What I do want booked is a cholesterol blood test, to see if the atorvastatin 40 is actually hitting the mark.

[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): I can do the cholesterol one. Last time they said it was better but nobody wrote the number in my book, so I can't tell you the figure. Do I have to starve, because my wife can drop me early on a Tuesday, before porridge.

[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes, fasting, water only from the night before. Tuesday is fine, we'll get it booked. I'm not giving you a painkiller for that throb, the aspirin you already tolerate stays, but no extra painkiller, and you don't need an antibiotic either.

[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Good, I wouldn't have swallowed a pain tablet anyway. For the dizzy mornings, should I just get up slower? I already sit on the edge and count to twenty, she's very strict, she was a school secretary.

[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ja, keep that, sit, count, then stand, and don't walk off until it settles. Don't cut the amlodipine yourself. Write the home pressures, morning and evening, in a notebook, and bring it.

[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Notebook, not the newspaper, morning and evening. I'll check the batteries in the Clicks machine. My dad had high blood pressure too, and a stroke at 72, he didn't make it, so you can see why she fusses. I don't smoke, I stopped in 1998, and I don't drink, well, a sherry at Christmas, which she says still counts.

[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): That family history I hear, and stopping smoking matters more than the Christmas sherry. I want you back in six weeks with the notebook, not sooner unless something shifts. If the hand suddenly gets weaker, or the speech goes thick again, or you can't stand, you don't wait, you go to casualty the same day.

[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Six weeks, notebook, casualty if it goes bad. Thick like the first day, when I sounded drunk and I hadn't touched a thing? The name-forgetting I can live with, I just point until the word arrives.

[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): Thick means slurred, or you can't get a sentence out, like day one. The pausing for names, if it stays as it is, we watch it. I'm happy calling this a stable recovery from a mild stroke, pressure a bit high on today's reading, and that possible drug rash still unresolved in the background.

[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Unresolved, ja. I'll try to find the old Victoria paper, it might name the antibiotic. It was a long time ago, maybe 2014, or 2016, I mix those years up completely. If I find it I'll bring it in six weeks.

[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): Bring it if you find it, and if you can't we just stay careful. Anything else, sleep, mood, the waterworks? No, actually, don't, I think out loud and we've covered what we needed today.

[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): The amlodipine box definitely says 5 mg, I read it twice this morning, not 10. The statin used to be 20 and they lifted it to 40 after the stroke, and I stayed on 40. I've also been doing the putty and the clothes pegs the physio showed me in hospital, most days, unless my wife doesn't nag, which she always does.

[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): 5 and 40, we're aligned, I won't change either dose today. If the cholesterol comes back high we might talk about going up, but only then, not today. Keep the putty and the pegs going, most days is enough, just don't strain until it hurts.

[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): Putty, pegs, no straining, six weeks, fasting bloods. I'll skip the large coffee next time so you get a fair pressure. Tell the sister at the desk I'm the slow one with the newspaper, she'll laugh.
[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): You're not the slow one, the clinic is. Go carefully to the car, and sit a moment if you stand and it swims. See you in six weeks.

spec.situation: Patient three months after a mild stroke with a spouse; slight weakness in the left hand; takes aspirin, atorvastatin and an amlodipine tablet; blood pressure read aloud; walking and speech discussed.

traps.happens: The doctor asks about drug reactions. Variants (use ONE per encounter): (a) the patient says 'No, never, I have taken penicillin and everything' (no allergy); (b) the patient is unsure ('maybe the antibiotic or the painkiller, nobody told me which'); (c) a real allergy with the reaction described; (d) allergies are never asked.
traps.label_rule: (a) NO allergy entry: negative_findings 'Allergies' absent. (b) allergy with status uncertain, the substance as described, the reaction if said, plus an allergy_uncertain uncertainty. (c) allergy with the reaction. (d) nothing at all. NEVER list a medicine the patient has taken without a reaction as an allergy, and the plan must not prescribe a drug of a recorded allergy's family.

traps.happens: The doctor asks only two to four review-of-systems questions (for example fever, weight, cough). Several other body systems are never asked about. One of the asked questions gets a vague or mixed answer.
traps.label_rule: negative_findings / review_of_systems ONLY for items the doctor actually asked AND the patient answered, evidence = that question and answer. Never add review-of-systems entries for systems nobody asked about, and never cite an unrelated turn (for example a turn about tiredness) for a system review.

features: doctor_changes_mind: the doctor says one plan, then changes it after new information; the label holds the final plan.

denial_then_admission: the patient first denies a symptom, then later describes it. The label records the symptom as present (the later, fuller answer) and does NOT also record the earlier denial as a negative finding.
